statement: In US adults who used only e-cigarettes every day (156 people), compared with adults who smoked only cigarettes every day (3,430), in the first wave (2013–2014) of the national PATH survey, the e-cigarette group said yes less often to each of four dependence questions: self-rated dependence 77.2% against 94.0%, strong cravings 72.8% against 86.9%, difficulty keeping from using where it was prohibited 5.6% against 28.6%, and feeling they really needed to use 71.5% against 88.5% (adjusted odds ratios for the cigarette group 2.85 to 6.92, every interval excluding 1); they also waited longer after waking before first use (adjusted geometric mean 29.2 against 20.0 minutes) (Liu et al., 2017). Dependence symptoms were therefore common among adults who only vaped every day, and less common than among adults who only smoked every day. Other surveys, read only as the National Academies describe them, point the same way (a 2012–2013 US telephone survey of 124 against 3,963 adults; a second analysis of the same PATH wave; a voluntary web survey of 3,609 people who vaped daily and recalled their earlier smoking), as do 2021 surveys of young people in England (52.5% of 16–19-year-olds who vaped rated themselves a little or very dependent, against 83% of those who smoked; McNeill et al., 2022). The National Academies judged the evidence that vaping results in dependence symptoms substantial, that the risk and severity are lower than for cigarettes moderate, and that product features (device type, nicotine concentration, flavouring, brand) are an important determinant moderate (the committee's judgments; the UK review restates them); the Australian review judged the evidence in people who smoke limited and in people who do not smoke substantial (Banks et al., 2023). Where product features were measured, in a voluntary web survey, higher dependence scores went with larger, more advanced devices and with a higher nicotine concentration of the liquid. These are one-time surveys with no follow-up. Nearly all of the e-cigarette group (92.9%) had smoked before and earlier smoking was not adjusted for; the people who keep vaping daily are a small selected share of those who try it; one item (difficulty refraining where use is prohibited) is a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes; there is no agreed scale for comparing the two; the surveys date from 2012–2014 and cannot speak to newer products such as nicotine-salt liquids and disposables, which the UK and Australian reviews describe as little studied; and nothing read follows dependence over time or compares dependence on vaping with dependence on smoking in people who have never smoked. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a large US survey from 2013 to 2014, adults who only vaped every day reported signs of dependence less often than adults who only smoked every day: 77 in 100 rated themselves as dependent, against 94 in 100 of those who smoked, and 6 in 100 found it hard to go without where use was banned, against 29 in 100. Other surveys in the US and England pointed the same way. So daily vaping was linked to dependence, but to less of it than daily smoking. Nearly all the people who vaped had smoked before, the surveys are one-off snapshots from before newer products such as disposables became common, and no study read can say how dependent a person who never smoked becomes.
population: Adults in the United States who used only e-cigarettes, or only cigarettes, every day (PATH Wave 1, 2013–2014); young people aged 11 to 19 in England (2021 surveys); other adult surveys as described by the National Academies
outcome: Dependence symptoms (self-rated dependence, strong cravings, difficulty keeping from using where prohibited, feeling a need to use, time to first use after waking) and dependence index scores
magnitude: Daily e-cigarette-only (n = 156) vs daily cigarette-only (n = 3,430), PATH Wave 1, weighted: self-rated dependence 77.2% vs 94.0% (adjusted odds ratio for the cigarette group 6.92, 95% CL 4.46–10.73); strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9% (2.85, 1.92–4.23); difficulty keeping from using where prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6% (6.39, 2.85–14.32); felt they really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5% (3.89, 2.36–6.40); time to first use after waking, adjusted geometric mean 29.16 (24.39–34.87) vs 20.03 (18.66–21.49) minutes (editors' calculation: ratio 1.46). As described by the National Academies: US National Adult Tobacco Survey 2012–2013, daily e-cigarette-only n = 124 vs cigarette-only n = 3,963, every symptom less common in the e-cigarette group (for example use within 30 minutes of waking 46.1%, 35.1–57.4); PATH Wave 1 item-response index, e-cigarette-only (n = 437) 1.37 SD units below cigarette-only (n = 8,689); web survey of 3,609 people who vaped daily, index 8.1 vs 14.5 for recalled smoking. England 2021, 16–19-year-olds: rated themselves a little or very dependent 52.5% of those who vaped vs 83% of those who smoked (McNeill et al., 2022).

evidence.extracted: In the 2013–2014 PATH Wave 1 adult survey, 156 adults who used only e-cigarettes every day and 3,430 who smoked only cigarettes every day (weighted shares of the analysis sample 4.6% and 95.4%) answered four yes/no questions. The e-cigarette group said yes less often to each (weighted, each p < 0.0001): considered themselves addicted 77.2% vs 94.0%; ever had strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9%; found it difficult in the past 12 months to keep from using where it was prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6%; ever felt they really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5%. First use within 5 minutes of waking 15.1% vs 24.0%; after more than 60 minutes 10.9% vs 12.1%.

Adjusted odds ratios for the cigarette group against the e-cigarette group (95% CL), adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and poverty status: addicted 6.92 (4.46–10.73); strong cravings 2.85 (1.92–4.23); difficult to refrain where prohibited 6.39 (2.85–14.32); really needed to use 3.89 (2.36–6.40). Time to first use after waking, geometric mean in minutes, adjusted (home smoking rules added): 29.16 (24.39–34.87) in the e-cigarette group vs 20.03 (18.66–21.49) in the cigarette group; unadjusted 23.46 (19.47–28.27) vs 19.25 (18.25–20.30). Editors' calculation: ratio of adjusted geometric means 1.46.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Ascertainment of Study Population, 5th paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Of the 156 in the e-cigarette group, 145 (92.9%) had formerly smoked cigarettes at the survey's established level, 10 (6.7%) had only experimented with smoking and 1 (0.4%) had never used any tobacco product. The authors state that over three quarters of the group considered themselves addicted, and that only 6.8% of adults who had ever tried an e-cigarette used one daily against 23.8% of adults who had tried a cigarette and smoked daily, so the exclusive daily comparison picks the most dependent people who vape. The groups also differed on poverty (below the poverty level 14.6% vs 35.0%) and on home rules (use allowed anywhere at any time at home 61.9% vs 26.5%).

The authors name as limits that amount used per day could not be compared (the units for e-cigarettes and cigarettes differ, because e-cigarette products vary in device, liquid nicotine concentration and flavour), that duration of use could not be reliably calculated, and that most adults who had used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days also used other products, so dependence is hard to attribute to one product (they were excluded). They call for future studies of exposure biomarkers such as cotinine and of how dependence develops over time and differs by device and liquid characteristics, noting that the longitudinal design of PATH will help. Editors' reading: the dependence items are self-reported; the design is a single survey wave, so nothing follows people over time.

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies: the 2012–2013 National Adult Tobacco Survey (a representative US telephone survey, identical wording for each product) compared 124 adults who used only e-cigarettes every day with 3,963 who smoked only cigarettes every day. Each dependence symptom was significantly less common in the e-cigarette group (for example use within 30 minutes of waking 46.1%, 95% CI 35.1–57.4; withdrawal symptoms 22.8%, 14.8–33.4) and not significantly different from people who smoked cigars daily (131). The committee notes that comparisons were not adjusted for prior tobacco history or demographics and that the market then held early-model devices.

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 3rd to 7th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The committee's account of Liu et al. (2017) repeats its figures (156 vs 3,430; 77.2% vs 94.0%; 5.6% vs 28.6%) and reads it as strong evidence that dependence symptoms are fairly high among adults who only vape every day but not as high as among adults who only smoke every day. Its limits: prior tobacco history was not adjusted for (92.9% of the e-cigarette group had smoked), so group differences may reflect earlier exposure, and the item on difficulty refraining where use is prohibited is probably a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes because fewer places restrict them (61.9% of the e-cigarette group could use theirs anywhere at home, against 26.5% of the cigarette group).
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 8th to 11th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies: a separate analysis of PATH Wave 1 (437 adults who used only e-cigarettes in the past year, daily or not, and 8,689 who only smoked cigarettes) used a 16-item dependence index tested for equal validity across products. Average severity was 1.37 standard deviation units lower for the e-cigarette-only group than for the cigarette-only group, comparable to cigar-only and higher among daily than non-daily e-cigarette-only participants (difference 0.40 SD). 3 of the 24 items were dropped as invalid indicators and 16 were retained as having minimal or no differential validity across products. The sample partly overlaps Liu et al. (same survey wave; this analysis included daily and non-daily users, Liu et al. daily users); the committee calls the two non-redundant data sources, but the editors count them as one dataset.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Anonymous Web Surveys of E-Cigarette Users, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As described by the National Academies: a voluntary anonymous web survey (December 2012 to August 2014; 3,609 people who vaped every day and had not smoked in the past 30 days, recruited on vaping and medical websites; 42% reported advocating for e-cigarettes online) compared dependence on e-cigarettes with their recall of earlier smoking: mean index 8.1 (SD 3.5) vs 14.5 (3.7). E-cigarette scores were higher with longer use, larger devices with a button, higher price and a higher nicotine concentration of the liquid. A second analysis of the same data (1,048 first-generation vs 3,373 advanced devices) found higher scores with advanced devices (8.3 vs 7.1 with first-generation) and a shorter time to first use after waking (38.7 vs 67.3 minutes), although their liquid had a lower nicotine concentration (15.1 vs 19.1 mg/mL). The committee notes the sample is not representative and that recall of earlier smoking could bias the comparison.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is substantial evidence that e-cigarette use results in symptoms of dependence on e-cigarettes, resting on several supportive findings from good-quality observational studies with very few or no credible opposing findings (symptoms of appreciable prevalence or severity; more frequent or longer use goes with more symptoms), supported by abuse-liability studies. This is the committee's judgment.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is moderate evidence that the risk and severity of dependence are lower for e-cigarettes than for combustible cigarettes, resting on several supportive findings from fair-quality studies with very few or no credible opposing findings; chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out. This is the committee's judgment.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)

evidence.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is moderate evidence that variability in product characteristics (nicotine concentration, flavouring, device type and brand) is an important determinant of the risk and severity of e-cigarette dependence: some findings link nicotine concentration, flavouring, device generation and brand to outcomes indicating dependence risk, with very few or no credible opposing findings. This is the committee's judgment.

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 5: Nicotine › Main findings › Nicotine dependency, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Main findings page › 5. Nicotine, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The UK review states that there was substantial evidence from previous reports (National Academies, the Committee on Toxicity and its own 2018 report) that vaping can result in symptoms of nicotine dependency, and moderate evidence that the risk and severity are lower than for cigarette smoking and vary with product characteristics such as device type and nicotine concentration; its pharmacokinetic review is consistent with this. It adds that many scales are used and there is no consensus on the best scale for vaping dependence, which makes comparison with smoking difficult, and cites a systematic review suggesting higher nicotine concentrations might increase abuse potential and appeal. The grading statements rest on earlier reports and existing evidence, not a new independent finding; the point about scales is this review's own finding.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 3: Vaping among young people › Main findings › Perceived addiction and urges to vape, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In the 2021 ITC Youth survey of 16–19-year-olds in England, 52.5% of those who currently vaped felt a little or very addicted to vaping (42.8% did not) against 83% of those who currently smoked who felt a little or very addicted to smoking (14.5% did not). Urges almost daily or more: 44.5% of those who vaped (16.8% never) against 66.6% of those who smoked (urges daily or several times a day; 4.7% never). In the 2021 ASH-Y survey of 11–18-year-olds, 41.5% of those who vaped had no urges and 23.5% strong to extremely strong urges, against 24.3% and 31.4% of those who smoked. The summary page does not say the groups were exclusive or adjusted.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Summary page › Chapter 5: Nicotine › Implications › Improved surveillance and further research, 4th to 6th paragraphs; Need for global standards and protocols, 1st paragraph; Chapter 3 › Implications › Further monitoring and research, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The UK review states that dependence on vaping assessed in 2021 appears lower than on smoking for young people and that further research is needed on dependence by type of product, nicotine type and nicotine strength. It calls for longitudinal studies of how dependence changes with experience, for measurements across products in people who have never smoked and start nicotine through vaping, and for a global consensus on how to measure dependence so that vaping and smoking can be compared.
evidence.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)

evidence.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, row 'Dependence and abuse liability (52)'; Box 2, same row
evidence.extracted: The Australian umbrella and top-up review (52 studies on dependence and abuse liability: 13 randomised trials, 1 cohort, 17 non-randomised intervention studies, 21 cross-sectional surveys) rates substantial evidence that nicotine e-cigarette use leads to dependence on e-cigarettes in people who do not smoke; in people who smoke, limited evidence that it leads to dependence, limited evidence that abuse liability is lower than for cigarettes or higher than for nicotine replacement products, and insufficient evidence that abuse liability is influenced by flavour and nicotine content. This is graded more cautiously than the National Academies' moderate rating for the comparison with cigarettes.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional self-report comparisons (card sc_liu_2017: ROBINS-E overall high). The e-cigarette group is selected (nearly all had formerly smoked; few of those who try e-cigarettes use them daily) and prior tobacco history, length of use and amount per day are not adjusted for; one item is a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes. The other surveys are read only through the National Academies' account, which itself flags a non-representative web sample with recall of earlier smoking.

inconsistency.note: Every source read points the same way; the size of the gap differs by item and survey.

indirectness.note: The data are from surveys of 2012–2014, before newer products such as nicotine-salt liquids and disposables were common (the National Academies call generalizability to products of that time questionable, and the UK and Australian reviews list newer products and dependence by product type as little studied); several sources are second-hand, and the UK review's dependence statements restate National Academies and earlier reports (counted once, as are the two PATH analyses).

imprecision.note: Intervals on the adjusted odds ratios exclude 1; the smallest e-cigarette groups are 124 and 156 people.

large_effect.note: Adjusted odds ratios are 2.85 to 6.92, but the biases that remain (selection of people who stay with e-cigarettes after smoking; prior tobacco history not adjusted) run away from the null, so no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational (cross-sectional survey) evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. The National Academies rate the lower-dependence comparison moderate and the dependence finding substantial, and the UK review repeats those ratings; these are the authors' judgments over mixed study types, not a GRADE rating, and overlapping reports and the two PATH analyses are counted once. Status replicated rests on independent datasets (US telephone survey, PATH, a web survey, English youth surveys) that agree on direction, three of them known here only through the reviews.
